notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0162.stoa023.opp-la: The Latin is a poor scan with many misread letters. The Hebrew words that stood in the empty parentheses are lost; only Jerome’s Latin transliterations (SIIM, ONIM, IIM, THENNIM) survive. A page number (175) and footnote marks in the text are not translated. iurare is read as intrare (“enter”).

nodes.text: (Verses 20–22.) “Nor will the Arab pitch his tents there, nor will shepherds rest there; but wild beasts will be there, their houses will be filled with serpents, and ostriches will live there, and hairy ones will dance there. And owls will answer in its dwellings, and Sirens in the shrines of pleasure.” Babylon will be so devastated and deserted that it will not be of use even as pasture for herds or flocks. For neither Arab nor Saracen will stretch out his tents there, nor will shepherds, weary with toil, rest there as they follow the tracks of their flocks; but among the broken walls and narrow passages of the old ruins *siim* will dwell, which the Septuagint alone translated “beasts”; the others [kept] the very name that is written in the Hebrew, wanting kinds of demons or phantoms to be understood. “And the houses,” he says, “will be filled”, as we have rendered it, “with serpents”; as Aquila translated, “with typhons”; as Symmachus, *onim*, giving the Hebrew word itself; but the Septuagint and Theodotion interpreted it as “cries” or “noises”. And as for what follows, “Hairy ones will dance there”, they understand either incubi, or satyrs, or certain wild men of the woods, whom some call *fatui ficarii* [fig-tree fauns], or kinds of demons. For “owls” too, all [kept] the Hebrew word itself, *iim*; the Septuagint alone translated “onocentaurs”. The Sirens are called *thennim*, which we interpret either as demons, or certain monsters, or at any rate great serpents, which are crested and fly. By all these, signs of desolation and solitude are shown: that the depopulation of a city once most powerful is so great that, because of the multitude of demons and beasts, none of the shepherds, that is, no one who seeks out the desert, dares to enter it. We have learned from a certain brother, an Elamite, who came out of those regions and now lives the life of the monks at Jerusalem, that there are royal hunting-grounds in Babylon, and that beasts of every kind are confined only by the circuit of its walls.
